introduction_markdown:
This paper is arranged in three sections, A, B and C. Section A: answer ALL 5 questions; you will be graded for the best 4 answers. Section B: answer ALL 2 questions in this section. Section C: answer 2 questions out of 3; if you attempt more than 2 questions, only the first two will be considered. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

**Useful data:** relative atomic masses H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0, N = 14.0; 1 faraday = 96000 coulombs; molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24000 cm$^3$; specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$; Avogadro number = $6.02\times10^{23}$; $0^\circ$C = 273 K.

questions.corrige_markdown:
(The first reagent is printed as $\mathrm{KBr_2}$; it should read $2\mathrm{KBr}$: $2\mathrm{KBr(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{KCl(aq)} + \mathrm{Br_2(aq)}$, balanced.)

**Reaction type:** a **displacement reaction** (a halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its salt). It is also a **redox reaction**: chlorine is reduced ($\mathrm{Cl_2} + 2e^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl^-}$) and bromide ions are oxidised ($2\mathrm{Br^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Br_2} + 2e^-$). Chlorine is more reactive than bromine.

**Observations:** when chlorine (greenish-yellow gas or chlorine water) is bubbled into the colourless potassium bromide solution, the solution turns **orange or brown** because bromine is formed.

**Reaction type:** a **redox reaction**: copper(II) oxide is **reduced** to copper (it loses oxygen) and hydrogen is **oxidised** to water (it gains oxygen); hydrogen is the reducing agent.

**Observations:** hydrogen is passed over heated copper(II) oxide; the **black solid turns brown (pink-brown) copper**, and **droplets of a colourless liquid (water)** condense on the cooler parts of the tube. The excess hydrogen is burnt at the end of the tube.

**Reaction type:** an **addition reaction** (hydrogenation) of an alkene: the double bond of ethene is broken and two hydrogen atoms are added, giving the saturated alkane ethane. It takes place with a **nickel catalyst at about $150^\circ$C**.

**Observations:** there is no striking colour change (all substances are colourless gases); the **volume of the gas mixture decreases** as the product forms. The product (saturated) no longer decolourises bromine water or acidified potassium manganate(VII), unlike ethene.

**Reaction type:** **esterification** (a condensation reaction): an alcohol (ethanol) reacts with a carboxylic acid (ethanoic acid) to give an ester (**ethyl ethanoate**) and water. It is **reversible** (the sign $\rightleftharpoons$), so the mixture contains all four substances at equilibrium; the reverse reaction is hydrolysis of the ester.

**Conditions and observations:** a few drops of **concentrated sulphuric acid** are added as a catalyst and the mixture is warmed (under reflux). The product is recognised by its **sweet, fruity smell**; poured into water, the ester forms a **colourless oily layer** on the surface.
